formation.title: The Unification of Hausaland
formation.text:
The ancient Hausa Bakwai, the seven true city-states born of the Bayajidda legend, have at last been brought under one rule. Kano, Katsina, Zazzau, Daura, Gobir, Rano, and Biram: each renowned for its own strengths, each now part of a greater whole. The question that faces us is what kind of nation we shall build from these proud cities. Shall we follow the path of Queen Amina, expanding our borders by the sword and shielding our people behind walls of earth and iron? Or shall we turn our energies to the great markets and trade routes that already make our cities the envy of the Sahel, becoming the commercial heart of West Africa?

This choice unlocks a destiny path in the Traditions tab.

options.text: Build the walls. Ride the horses. Conquer.

modifiers.name: Walls of Amina
modifiers.text: In the tradition of Queen Amina of Zazzau, we shall expand our domain through force of arms, building walls around every city we conquer and securing the trade routes with cavalry and iron.

options.text: The caravans bring more wealth than any army.

modifiers.name: Crossroads of the Sahel
modifiers.text: The wealth of nations flows through our markets. From the gold fields of the south to the salt mines of the Sahara, every caravan that crosses the Sahel enriches our coffers and spreads our fame.

advances.name: Birni Fortification
advances.text: The construction of massive earthen walls around Hausa cities, creating fortified urban centers that could withstand prolonged sieges.

advances.name: Bayajidda Legacy
advances.text: The founding myth of the Hausa Bakwai, seven city-states descended from the hero Bayajidda, provides the cultural framework for Hausa political identity.

advances.name: Sahel Agriculture
advances.text: The development of agricultural techniques suited to the Sahel environment, centering on cereals, cotton, vegetables, and livestock, with metalworking to produce the tools needed for cultivation.

advances.name: Spread of Islam
advances.text: The arrival of Islam through trans-Saharan merchants transformed urban Hausa society, introducing literacy, legal traditions, and connections to the wider Islamic world.

advances.name: Equestrian Nobility
advances.text: The Hausa aristocracy developed a horse-riding culture that became the foundation of their military power. Every sarki and titled lord rides to war with his barade, the mounted champions of his household.

advances.name: The Kano Chronicle
advances.text: One of Africa's most important historical documents, the Kano Chronicle records the city's history from its legendary founding through the reigns of its kings.

event.title: The Kano Chronicle
event.text: Our scholars have compiled a chronicle of the kings of Kano, tracing the lineage of our rulers from the legendary Bagauda to the present day. Written in Arabic script, this remarkable document records the rise and fall of dynasties, the coming of Islam, the great wars and alliances that shaped our nation, and the deeds of kings both wise and foolish. It is one of the great historical works of our continent, a testament that our civilization has a story worth telling and preserving for the ages.

modifiers.name: Chronicle of Kings
modifiers.text: The written record of our history lends authority to our dynasty and inspires pride in our people. Our deeds are set down for posterity.

advances.name: Indigo Dyeing
advances.text:
The establishment of the famous dye pits of Kano, producing vibrant indigo-dyed cloth that became one of Hausaland's most valued exports.

Available in: Kofar Mata Dye Pits

advances.name: Yan Lifida Tradition
advances.text: The development of the Yan Lifida, elite heavy cavalry wearing layered quilted cotton armor with chain mail, as the premier military force of the Hausa states.

advances.name: Rumfa's Reforms
advances.text: The transformative governance reforms of Muhammad Rumfa of Kano, who built mosques and madrasas, established market regulations, and elevated Kano into a center of Islamic scholarship.

event.title: The Reforms of Muhammad Rumfa
event.text: Muhammad Rumfa, Sarki of Kano, has transformed our greatest city into a center of Islamic learning and governance. He has built mosques and madrasas, invited scholars from Egypt, Tunis, and Morocco, and commissioned the great scholar al-Maghili to write a treatise on the obligations of Muslim rulers. The Taqaddum, Rumfa's code of governance, establishes market regulations, court protocols, and the framework for a just Islamic state. This is not merely a reform of administration; it is the elevation of our entire civilization.

options.text: Embrace the path of learning and faith.

modifiers.name: Rumfa's Enlightenment
modifiers.text: Following the model of Muhammad Rumfa, our commitment to Islamic learning and good governance has elevated our civilization and attracted scholars from across the Muslim world.

options.text: Centralize authority in the Sarki's court.

modifiers.name: Political Centralization
modifiers.text: The reforms of Muhammad Rumfa concentrate authority in the Sarki's court, creating a more efficient administration that can govern the complex affairs of a growing state.

advances.name: Trans-Saharan Links
advances.text: The establishment of Kano and Katsina as major nodes in the trans-Saharan trade network, connecting gold-producing regions with North Africa.

advances.name: Queen Amina's Campaigns
advances.text: Queen Amina of Zazzau waged a 34-year campaign of conquest, extending Hausa territory from Bauchi to Nupe and building fortification walls across the land.

advances.name: Sarauta Governance
advances.text: The formalization of the sarauta system of governance, organizing administration through the Sarki and a council of nine elders representing royal, clerical, and commercial interests.

advances.name: Leather Exports
advances.text:
The development of Hausa leatherwork into a major export industry, with industrial-scale indigo processing to dye the leather and cloth that made Kano famous.

Available in: Kofar Mata Dye Pits

advances.name: Artisan Guilds
advances.text:
The organization of Hausa artisans into specialized guilds (blacksmiths, weavers, dyers, leatherworkers, and builders), each with internal governance and market privileges. The builders shape tubali, the sun-dried bricks of Hausa walls and vaults.

Available in: Kofar Mata Dye Pits

advances.name: Gobir Frontier
advances.text: The northernmost Hausa state of Gobir maintained a permanent military establishment to defend Hausaland against foreign invaders from the Sahara. Behind its horsemen stand the yan baka, country bowmen whose arrows are poisoned.

advances.name: Gunpowder Adoption
advances.text: The adoption of firearms through trans-Saharan trade, creating musketeer infantry (Yan Bindiga) to complement the traditional cavalry forces.

advances.name: Majema Leatherwork
advances.text: The refinement of Hausa leatherworking by the majema artisans, using vegetable-based tanning with bagaruwa pods to produce fine leather goods for export.

advances.name: Market Competition
advances.text: The rivalry between Katsina and Kano for dominance of trans-Saharan trade, driving both cities to develop sophisticated market institutions.

advances.name: Ajami Scholarship
advances.text: The development of Hausa ajami, writing the Hausa language in Arabic script, creating a literate scholarly class that produced legal, historical, and religious works.

advances.name: Zango Networks
advances.text:
The establishment of zango, resident Hausa merchant communities, along major trade routes from the forest belt to the Sahara, extending commercial influence far beyond Hausaland. The mail and iron they bring home go into the quilted armor of the cavalry.

Lifida Armoring is available in: Kofar Mata Dye Pits

advances.name: Centralized Sarauta
advances.text: The consolidation of royal authority under strong sarki who centralized tax collection and military command, strengthening the state apparatus.

advances.name: Urban Growth
advances.text: The expansion of Hausa cities into major urban centers, with Kano and Katsina rivaling Timbuktu in population and commercial activity.

advances.name: Cotton Industry
advances.text:
The development of cotton agriculture and textile weaving as a major industry, with Hausa cloth traded throughout West Africa.

Available in: Kofar Mata Dye Pits

advances.name: Standing Army
advances.text: The evolution of Hausa military organization from ad hoc levies to permanent standing forces in the major city-states, first among them the dogarai, the palace guard that answers to the sarki alone.

advances.name: Sahel Diplomacy
advances.text: Hausa diplomatic traditions of negotiation and alliance-building between city-states, managing the complex balance of power across the Sahel.

advances.name: Defense of Autonomy
advances.text: The defense of Hausa city-state independence against external pressures, preserving the traditions of self-governance that defined Hausaland.

advances.name: Commercial Sophistication
advances.text:
The continued refinement of Hausa commercial institutions, with market towns serving as centers of regional and long-distance trade. The red goatskin of the Hausa tanners is sold in Europe as Morocco leather.

Available in: Majema Tannery

advances.name: Cultural Resilience
advances.text: The preservation and development of Hausa cultural identity through oral tradition, distinctive architecture, and specialized craft production. At the festival every titled household rides past its ruler in the durbar, pageant and muster in one.

advances.name: Sahel Stewardship
advances.text: The expansion of agricultural techniques to manage the fragile Sahel environment and sustain growing urban populations.

advances.name: Maliki Jurisprudence
advances.text: The development of a legal system combining Islamic jurisprudence of the Maliki school with Hausa customary law, creating a pragmatic governance framework.

destiny.name: Destiny of Hausaland
destiny.text: The Hausa Bakwai are united under one banner. Now we must prove that this union was not an accident of history but the beginning of something greater. Stability and order are the first requirements.

conditions.text: Stability at least 25

event.title: The Destiny of Hausaland
event.text: The seven true states are united, and a single Sarki rules from the greatest city in the western Sudan. But unity is only the beginning. The world beyond our walls is vast, and the path we choose now will shape the destiny of our people for generations. The foundations are laid. Now we must build.

destiny.name: The Sword Rides South and North
destiny.text: In the tradition of Queen Amina, we shall extend our dominion beyond the Hausa heartland. The Nupe kingdoms to the south and the Tuareg of Air to the north must both acknowledge our supremacy.

conditions.text: Chose Walls of Amina
Stability at least 25
Own Bida, or a subject owns it
Own Agadez, or a subject owns it

event.title: Nupe and Air Submit
event.text: Our cavalry has ridden south to the banks of the Niger and north to the oases of Air. The Nupe princes and the Tuareg chiefs have learned what Queen Amina taught their ancestors centuries ago: that the Hausa ride where they please, and those who resist are broken. The trade routes to the south and the caravan paths to the north now flow through territory under our protection.

destiny.name: Conquest of Bornu and Oyo
destiny.text: The great rival kingdoms of Bornu and Oyo stand as the only obstacles to Hausa hegemony in the western Sudan. Their capitals must fall to our armies, and four of our towns must be walled as Amina walled hers.

conditions.text: Own Ngazargamu, or a subject owns it
Own Ọ̀yọ́ Ile, or a subject owns it
At least 4 of our locations have Birni Walls or City Walls (City Walls stand only in cities)

event.title: The Fall of Bornu and Oyo
event.text: The two great rival kingdoms that hemmed in Hausaland for centuries have been brought to heel. Ngazargamu, the fortress-capital of the Bornu empire, has opened its gates to our forces. In the west, the great city of Oyo-Ile, seat of the Alaafin, acknowledges Hausa supremacy. We stand as the dominant power of the western Sudan. How shall we administer these conquests?

modifiers.name: Conqueror of Nations
modifiers.text: The submission of rival kingdoms to Hausa authority has granted us experience in managing conquered peoples and extracting tribute.

options.text: Forge the conquered into a single army.

modifiers.name: Iron Discipline
modifiers.text: Constant campaigning on the frontiers has hardened our troops and taught our commanders the art of maintaining fortifications with minimal expense.

destiny.name: Empire of the Sahel
destiny.text: From Timbuktu to Benin, from the Niger bend to the forests of the south, a Hausa empire shall unite the western Sudan under one crown, with eight of its towns behind birni walls. This is the culmination of Amina's vision.

conditions.text: Own Timbuktu, or a subject owns it
Own Djenné, or a subject owns it
Own Benin, or a subject owns it
At least 8 of our locations have Birni Walls or City Walls (City Walls stand only in cities)
Prestige at least 75

event.title: Empire of the Sahel
event.text: From the ancient libraries of Timbuktu to the bronze workshops of Benin, from the scholarly mosques of Djenne to the great markets of Kano, a Hausa empire now stretches across the western Sudan. Not since the days of Songhai and Mali has a single power commanded such territory in West Africa. We have fulfilled the vision of Queen Amina and surpassed it a hundredfold. How shall history remember this achievement?

options.text: We shall administer this empire wisely.

modifiers.name: Sahelian Imperium
modifiers.text: The administration of a vast Sahelian empire requires sophisticated intelligence networks and the ability to project power quickly. The price of empire is eternal vigilance, and the tribes of the conquered lands resent the watch kept on them.

modifiers.name: Eternal Conquest
modifiers.text: The Hausa war machine has become a self-sustaining engine of expansion, recruiting new soldiers as fast as provinces are conquered. Diplomacy is an afterthought.

destiny.name: Cotton and Caravans
destiny.text: Our wealth begins with the cotton fields and dye pits that make Kano cloth famous across the continent. We must ensure that cotton flows through our markets and our treasury is full.

event.title: The Cotton Road
event.text: The markets of Kano overflow with cotton: raw from the fields, spun into thread, woven into cloth, and dyed the deep indigo that has become our trademark. Caravans carry our textiles north across the Sahara and south to the forest kingdoms. The wealth that flows through our hands proves that a bale of cotton can be worth more than a captured city. Our treasury grows, and with it our influence.

destiny.name: Crossroads of Empires
destiny.text: Hausaland sits at the crossroads of every major trade route in the western Sudan. By digging the indigo dye pits of Kano, whose cloth the caravans come for, and building up Katsina, where the Saharan road ends, we can become the commercial heart of Africa.

event.title: The Crossroads Flourish
event.text: Hausaland has become what its geography always promised: the indispensable crossroads of West African commerce. Every caravan from the Sahara, every trade convoy from the forest belt, every merchant seeking gold, salt, leather, or textiles passes through our cities. Our indigo cloth is sold from Tripoli to the forest kingdoms, our markets are sophisticated, and our cities grow rich on the flow of goods. What shall we invest in?

options.text: Invest in our merchants and markets.

modifiers.name: Merchant Princes
modifiers.text: The great merchant houses of Kano and Katsina have invested heavily in cotton production, using their wealth to shape policy. Military spending is kept lean.

options.text: Invest in scholars and diplomatic ties.

modifiers.name: Scholarly Exchange
modifiers.text: The flow of scholars and diplomats through Hausa cities has strengthened our ties to the wider world and brought new knowledge to our courts.

destiny.name: The Great Market
destiny.text: Let Kano and Katsina be spoken of alongside the great markets of the world. With salt from the Sahara flowing through our markets, Kano grown to twice its old size and our treasury overflowing, we shall build a commercial empire that outlasts any conqueror.

event.title: The Great Market of Kano
event.text: They say that everything in the world can be bought in the great market of Kano: salt from the Sahara, kola from the forests, leather worked so fine that Europeans call it Morocco leather without knowing it came from our tanneries, cloth dyed the deepest indigo, iron tools, horses, books, and goods from lands most people have never heard of. Our commercial empire is the envy of Africa. How shall we use this wealth?

modifiers.name: Emporium of Africa
modifiers.text: Hausaland has become the indispensable commercial hub of West Africa, its merchants and diplomats welcome in every court, its markets drawing traders from across the known world.

options.text: Become patrons of learning and the arts.

modifiers.name: Patron of Learning
modifiers.text: The investment in scholarship and Islamic learning has expanded our horizons and deepened our understanding of the world, though our military readiness has suffered somewhat.

units.name: Yan Lifida
units.text: Elite Hausa heavy cavalry wearing layered quilted cotton armor (lifida) and chain mail (sulke), mounted on armored horses. These formidable warriors served as the emir's bodyguard and the shock force of Hausa armies.

units.name: Yan Lifida (Levy)
units.text: Levy-raised heavy cavalry drawn from the Hausa aristocracy, equipped with quilted armor and chain mail in the Yan Lifida tradition.

units.name: Yan Bindiga
units.text: Hausa musketeers armed with firearms acquired through trans-Saharan trade. These gunpowder infantry provided devastating firepower to complement the traditional cavalry charge.

units.name: Yan Bindiga (Levy)
units.text: Levy-raised musketeers equipped with trade firearms, drawn from the common soldiery of the Hausa city-states.

units.name: Barade
units.text: Mounted champions of the Hausa lords, lancers in gown and turban who ride ahead of the host and close fast.

units.name: Yan Baka
units.text: Country bowmen whose arrows are dipped in poison. A scratch is enough. They carry no shield and do not last once the enemy reaches them.

units.name: Dogarai
units.text: The palace guard of the sarki, household men always under arms who answer to him alone. Few in number and the last to leave a field.

buildings.name: Birni Walls
buildings.text: Massive earthen fortification walls enclosing entire Hausa cities and their agricultural hinterlands. The Kano walls alone stretched over 23 kilometers, reaching heights of 15 meters with a base thickness of 12 meters.

buildings.name: Kofar Mata Dye Pits
buildings.text: Circular dye pits producing the vibrant indigo-dyed cloth that made Kano famous throughout West Africa and across the Sahara. The purple cotton of Kano once rivaled the fabled riches of Timbuktu.

buildings.name: Tsangaya School
buildings.text: An Islamic study center where Quranic learning and Arabic literacy are taught, producing the literate scholarly class that administers the city-states and maintains legal and historical records.

buildings.name: Sarauta Council Hall
buildings.text: The seat of Hausa governance where the Sarki and his council of nine elders deliberate matters of state, balancing the interests of the crown, the clergy, and the merchant guilds.

buildings.name: Zango Trading Post
buildings.text: A Hausa diaspora trading station where resident merchants serve as way-stations for caravans and centers of commercial intelligence, extending Hausa trade networks far beyond the homeland.

buildings.name: Majema Tannery
buildings.text: A workshop of the majema leatherworkers, using traditional vegetable-based tanning with bagaruwa pods to produce the supple leather goods that made Hausaland famous across the Sahara and beyond.

buildings.name: Durbar Ground
buildings.text: The open ground before the palace where the hawan sallah is ridden. Each titled household parades its horsemen past the ruler in full trappings, and the ruler counts them.

buildings.name: Gidan Sarki
buildings.text: The Imperial Palace of the Sarki of all Hausaland, a magnificent complex combining the grandeur of a royal court with the military command infrastructure needed to govern a continental empire. Its walls echo with the authority of Amina's heirs.

buildings.name: Fatauci House
buildings.text: The grand trading hall of the fatauci, the chief merchant of the Hausa commercial network. From this building, the vast caravan routes stretching from the Sahara to the forests are coordinated, deals negotiated, and the wealth of nations counted.

list.name: Sarauta Council
list.text: The graded body of titled office-holders that surrounded the sarki of a Hausa birni: the Galadima as administrator of the capital and senior counsellor; the Madawaki as commander of the cavalry; the Waziri as president of council; the Sarkin Yaki as field marshal; the Magajin Gari and the mai unguwa as ward elders. Titles were appointive, not strictly hereditary, and the council of nine kingmakers (in Kano, the Tara-ta-Kano) confirmed each new sarki from among the eligible princes. The system gave the Hausa state a working aristocracy without primogeniture, but it also kept the ruler permanently dependent on the consent of his great titled men.

list.name: Alkali Court
list.text: The chief judge (the alkalin alkalai) presided over a hierarchy of Maliki qadis whose courts adjudicated inheritance, contract, family, and waqf matters according to the Mukhtasar of Khalil ibn Ishaq and the Risala of Ibn Abi Zayd. Maliki jurisprudence reached the Hausa cities through Wangara scholars in the fifteenth century and through Katsina's links with Timbuktu's Sankore tradition; under Muhammadu Korau (r. c. 1445-93) Katsina became the principal site of Islamic legal scholarship in Hausaland. The alkali courts ran in parallel with sarauta justice for non-Muslims, generating a productive tension that lasted until the jihad.

conditions.text: Sunnism religion

list.name: Kano Chronicle Office
list.text: The continuously-updated Arabic-language dynastic chronicle preserved at the sarki's court, listing each Kano ruler from the legendary Bagauda (c. 999) onward with date of accession, deeds in war, and the great events of the reign. The chronicle was no passive record but a working instrument of legitimacy, recited at each new installation and consulted to settle questions of rank and precedence. Sister chronicles (the Katsina chronicle, the Song of Bagauda, the Wangara Chronicle, the Rawdat al-afkar) joined it across the bakwai. Once entrenched, the chronicle's authority is hard to set aside, even when its scribes have grown careless.

list.name: Wangarawa Compact
list.text: The settled presence of Soninke-Wangara merchant-scholars in the great Hausa markets, whose caravans bound Hausaland to the Niger Bend, the salt mines of Taghaza, and the kola forests of Gonja. The Kano Chronicle records that under Sarki Yaji (r. c. 1349-85) the Wangarawa, perhaps as many as one hundred and sixty under Shaikh Abdurrahman Zaite, settled in Kano and brought Islam with them. Their successors anchored Katsina and Kano as sarakuman kasuwa ('kings of the market'), serving as commercial agents, moneylenders, and clerics-for-hire. The compact rests on light taxation and the courts' protection of foreign merchants; the indigenous Hausa nobility resented every concession.

conditions.text: Any of

list.name: Birnin Order
list.text: The walled-city order, by which the great earthen ramparts of the Hausa birane enclosed royal palace, central market, and densely-packed wards under the authority of ward-heads (mai unguwa). The Kano walls, begun under Gijimasu (r. c. 1095-1134) and completed under Kanajeji, rose ten to twelve metres in places and ranked among the largest in Africa. Birnin Zazzau, in part attributed to Queen Amina of Zaria (r. c. 1576), and the walls of Katsina and Daura kept the model. The mai unguwa reported tax, recruited the militia, and maintained the gates by night, turning the fortified shell into a working civic order.

list.name: Maguzawa Compact
list.text: The unwritten accommodation by which non-Muslim Hausa villages (the Maguzawa, 'those who fled' the conversions of the fifteenth century) were permitted to retain their bori shrines, their ancestral chieftaincies, and their seasonal festivals within Muslim-ruled birane. In return they paid a tribute of grain, cloth, and iron, and supplied levies to the sarki's wars. The compact was durable: it survived the Islamization of the courts, the rise of the alkali courts, and the long Bornu wars. Only the Sokoto jihad of 1804, which classified the Maguzawa as apostates rather than dhimmis, ended it.
